fields.title: Jeremiah
fields.subtitle: Yirmeyahu, “The Book of Jeremiah”
fields.description: The words of the weeping prophet, called as a youth “to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant”, who spent forty years warning Judah that Babylon was coming and watched Jerusalem burn. Broken cisterns and the temple sermon, the potter’s house and the yoke on his neck, the prophet’s own anguished prayers to God, a letter to the exiles telling them to seek the peace of the city, a scroll cut up and burned by a king, a cistern full of mud, and a field bought in a land about to fall. And at its heart the promise of a new covenant, God’s law written on the heart and sin remembered no more. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Jeremiah?
qa.answer: The second of the major prophets in the Old Testament, and by word count the longest book in the Bible. It gathers the messages of the prophet Jeremiah to Judah in its last forty years, from about 627 BC to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC and after, with stories of his life and sufferings. Its pieces are arranged by theme rather than by date: oracles against Judah (chapters 1–25), Jeremiah and the false prophets (26–29), the Book of Consolation (30–33), the last years and the fall (34–45), oracles against the nations (46–51) and a closing account of the fall of Jerusalem (52).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Jeremiah, and when?
qa.answer: The book presents itself as “the words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests at Anathoth” (1:1), spoken from the thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 627 BC, until after the fall of Jerusalem. Chapter 36 tells how Jeremiah dictated his messages to his scribe Baruch son of Neriah, and much of the story of his life may come from Baruch. The book exists in two ancient forms: the Hebrew text used by most Bibles and a shorter form, about an eighth shorter and arranged differently, preserved in the Greek Septuagint and some Dead Sea Scrolls. Scholars differ over how much later editing shaped the book, while agreeing that it gathers the words of the prophet and those closest to him.

qa.question: Why is Jeremiah called the weeping prophet?
qa.answer: Because he grieved so openly for his people and for himself. “If only my head were all water and my eyes a fountain of tears, so that I could weep day and night for the slain of my dear people!” (9:1). His book includes a series of raw personal prayers, often called his confessions (in chapters 11–20), in which he complains to God, wishes he had never been born and says the word of God burns in his bones like fire. Tradition also linked him with the book of Lamentations, the poems of grief over fallen Jerusalem, which follows Jeremiah in English Bibles.

qa.question: What is the new covenant in Jeremiah 31?
qa.answer: God’s promise in Jeremiah 31:31–34 to make “a new covenant” with Israel and Judah, unlike the one made at the exodus, which the people broke. This time God will write his instruction on their hearts, all of them will know him, “from the least to the greatest”, and he will forgive their guilt and remember their sin no more. It is the longest Old Testament passage quoted in the New Testament (Hebrews 8:8–12), and at the Last Supper Jesus called the cup “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). Christians believe the promise is fulfilled in Christ and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

qa.question: What does Jeremiah 29:11 mean?
qa.answer: The verse, “I have planned peace for you, not disaster, so as to give you a future and a hope”, comes from a letter Jeremiah sent to the Jews already taken captive to Babylon. False prophets were promising a quick return; Jeremiah told them to build houses, plant gardens, raise families and pray for the city where they lived, because the exile would last seventy years (29:10). The promise is not that hardship will be brief, but that God has not forgotten his people in it, and that those who seek him with all their heart will find him even there (29:13). Christians have rightly taken comfort from it, while reading it as the people it was first written to would have heard it.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The poetry, which makes up much of Jeremiah, is set out line by line, and “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
“I knew you before I shaped you in the womb; I set you apart before you came out of the womb; I have given you to the nations as a prophet.”

— Jeremiah 1:5

No prophet lets us closer than Jeremiah. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up; Ezekiel sees wheels full of eyes. Jeremiah tells us what it cost him to be a prophet at all: the nights of weeping, the friends who turned on him, the day he cursed the day he was born. He is called the weeping prophet, and he earned the name. But he is also the prophet of the new covenant, and the one who bought a field in a country about to be conquered because God told him that fields would be bought there again.

The book opens with a young man from a family of priests in Anathoth, a village a few miles north of Jerusalem, and a word that came to him “in the thirteenth year of Josiah’s reign”, about 627 BC. It runs for some forty years, through the last kings of Judah, the siege and burning of Jerusalem, and the scattering of its people. Jeremiah watched his nation die. He had spent his life telling it that it would, and asking it, in God’s name, to turn back before it was too late.

Jeremiah’s world

Jeremiah was born into a hopeful time. Josiah was the best king Judah had had in generations. In his eighteenth year a book of the law was found in the temple, and the king led a great reform: idols were torn down, the Passover was kept, and the covenant was renewed (2 Kings 22–23). Assyria, the empire that had swallowed the northern kingdom of Israel a century before, was crumbling.

Then everything went wrong at once. Josiah was killed in battle in 609 BC. His son Jehoiakim undid much of his father’s work and despised the prophet. Babylon, under Nebuchadnezzar, defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 and became the power of the age. In 597 it took Jerusalem, and carried off the young king Jehoiachin with the leading families, among them a priest named Ezekiel. Zedekiah, the last king, wavered between submitting and rebelling until Babylon lost patience. The city fell in 587 or 586 BC, after a siege of a year and a half; the temple Solomon had built was burned.

Through all of it Jeremiah said the same unwelcome thing. Babylon was coming as God’s instrument of judgement; resistance was useless; the only way to live was to submit, and the only hope was in God’s mercy beyond the disaster. To his hearers it sounded like treason, and they treated it so.

The shape of the book

Jeremiah is the longest book in the Bible by word count, and it is not arranged in order of time. Its pieces were gathered by theme and by collection, and a reader who expects a story told from start to finish will be lost by chapter 21. It helps to know the rough outline:

  • Chapters 1–25: the call, and the oracles against Judah and Jerusalem, mostly in poetry, with the prophet’s own laments woven in.
  • Chapters 26–29: Jeremiah against the false prophets: the temple sermon and his trial, the yoke on his neck, the letter to the exiles.
  • Chapters 30–33: the Book of Consolation, the great promises of restoration and the new covenant.
  • Chapters 34–45: the story of the last years, the siege and the fall, and what came after, much of it told by Jeremiah’s scribe Baruch.
  • Chapters 46–51: oracles against the nations, from Egypt to Babylon itself.
  • Chapter 52: a closing account of the fall of Jerusalem, close to the end of 2 Kings.

The book itself tells us how some of it was written. In chapter 36 Jeremiah dictates his messages to Baruch son of Neriah, who writes them on a scroll. There is also an older form of the book, preserved in the ancient Greek translation and among the Dead Sea Scrolls, that is roughly an eighth shorter and places the oracles against the nations in the middle. Scholars weigh the two forms differently; this translation follows the Hebrew text that most English Bibles use.

The call: to uproot and to plant

Jeremiah’s first words to God are an objection: “I do not know how to speak; I am a mere youth.” God does not argue with the description. He answers with a promise, “for I am with you to rescue you”, and a commission:

See, on this day I have set you over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant.”

— Jeremiah 1:10

Count the verbs: four to tear down, two to build. That proportion is the shape of Jeremiah’s ministry, and the pair returns through the book as a refrain. Most of his work will be demolition. But demolition is not the last word, and the last verb is “plant”.

Two visions follow. Jeremiah sees “a rod cut from an almond tree”, and God says, “I am keeping watch over my word until I carry it out.” In Hebrew the almond is shaqed and “keeping watch” is shoqed: the almond, the first tree to wake in the spring, becomes a pledge that God is awake to his word. Then a boiling pot tilted from the north: the disaster will come from that direction, and it will be Babylon.

Broken cisterns and a temple of words

The first oracles are a lawsuit. God remembers Israel’s first love, “how you loved me as a bride”, and asks what fault their ancestors found in him that they went so far away. Then comes one of the great images of the Bible:

For my people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the spring of living water, and cut out cisterns for themselves, cracked cisterns that can hold no water.

— Jeremiah 2:13

Idolatry, in Jeremiah, is not only wicked; it is foolish. It trades a living spring for a tank cut in rock that leaks. And the people have done it while going to church. In chapter 7 Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and tells the worshippers not to trust in the chant “This is the LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple!” They steal, murder, commit adultery and burn incense to Baal, and then come and stand in God’s house and say they are safe. God asks whether this house has become “a hideout for robbers in your eyes”, and tells them to go and look at Shiloh, where the sanctuary once stood and stood no longer. Six centuries later Jesus quoted these words as he drove the traders out of the temple courts (Mark 11:17).

For that sermon Jeremiah was nearly put to death. Chapter 26 tells how the priests and prophets demanded it, and how some of the elders remembered that Micah had said much the same in Hezekiah’s day and lived. A prophet named Uriah, who preached the same message, was not so fortunate. He fled to Egypt, and Jehoiakim had him brought back and killed.

The heart and its cure

Jeremiah’s diagnosis goes deeper than behaviour. The people say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace; they “have forgotten how to blush”; they cannot change. “Can a Cushite change his skin, or a leopard its spots?” And then the verse that has troubled and steadied readers ever since:

The heart is more devious than anything else, and it is past healing; who can understand it?

— Jeremiah 17:9

It is set beside a picture of the alternative. The one who trusts in mere human strength is “like a bare shrub in the desert”; the one who trusts in the LORD is “like a tree set out beside the water”, green in the heat and fruitful in drought (17:5–8). Jeremiah’s answer to a heart past healing is not a better heart of our own making. It is the promise, still fourteen chapters away, that God will write on hearts himself.

Meanwhile God pleads. The word that runs through these chapters is “return”. “Return, faithless Israel… I will not stay angry forever.” “Return, faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness.” The judgement Jeremiah announces is real, but it is announced so that it need not fall.

The confessions of Jeremiah

Scattered through chapters 11–20 are passages unlike anything else in the prophets: Jeremiah’s own prayers, raw with anger and grief, often called his confessions. He learns that the men of his own village are plotting to kill him: “I was like a trusting lamb being led away to be slaughtered.” He asks God why the wicked prosper, and God answers that worse is coming: “If you have raced with runners on foot and they have worn you out, how will you keep pace with horses?” He wishes he had never been born. He accuses God of being “like a stream that deceives”.

The last of them is the fiercest. “You enticed me, LORD, and I was taken in.” Everyone laughs at him; his message has made him a joke. He resolves to stop speaking, and finds he cannot:

If I say, “I will not mention him or speak in his name anymore,” then it is like a fire burning in my heart, shut up inside my bones. I wear myself out holding it in, and I cannot.

— Jeremiah 20:9

Within a few verses he moves from “the LORD is with me like a terrifying warrior” to a song of praise, and then straight to “A curse on the day I was born!” The book does not tidy this up. It leaves the prophet’s agony on the page, and in doing so gives every believer who has felt abandoned by God permission to say so to God. Jeremiah complains to God, not about him behind his back, and God answers him: “If you turn back, I will take you back, and you will stand before me.”

His life itself became part of the message. He was told not to marry or have children, because of what was coming on the children of that land (16:1–4). He was sent to the potter’s house, where a spoiled pot was reshaped on the wheel, and heard God say, “As the clay is in the potter’s hand, so you are in my hand, house of Israel.” He smashed a clay jar before the elders (19), wore a yoke on his neck to tell the nations to submit to Babylon (27), and watched the prophet Hananiah break it, only to be told that the wooden bars would be replaced with iron (28).

A letter to the exiles

After the first deportation in 597, Jeremiah wrote to the exiles in Babylon. Prophets there were promising a quick return. Jeremiah told them to settle in: “Build houses and settle down in them. Plant gardens and eat what they produce.” Marry, have children, increase. And more surprising still:

Seek the peace of the city where I have sent you as exiles, and pray to the LORD for it, since your own peace depends on its peace.

— Jeremiah 29:7

The famous promise of 29:11 belongs here, and its setting matters. “I have planned peace for you, not disaster, so as to give you a future and a hope” was spoken to people who would not see home, after the words “When Babylon’s seventy years have been completed, I will come to your aid.” It is not a promise that trouble will be short. It is a promise that God has not forgotten his people in it, and that those who seek him with all their heart will find him there, in Babylon.

The Book of Consolation

In chapters 30–33, as the city goes under, the tone changes. Jeremiah is told to write down words of restoration: the captives brought home, the city rebuilt, Rachel weeping for her children and told to hold back her tears, because “they will come back from the land of the enemy”. God speaks of Ephraim as “my dear son” and says, “my heart aches for him.” Then comes the passage for which the book is most remembered:

The days are coming, declares the LORD, and then I will make a covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah: a new covenant. It will not be like the covenant I made with their ancestors on the day I took their hand to lead them out from the land of Egypt. They broke my covenant, though I was their husband, declares the LORD. Rather, this will be the covenant that I make with the house of Israel when those days are past, declares the LORD: I will set my instruction deep inside them and write it on their hearts. I will be their God, and they will be my people.

— Jeremiah 31:31–33

The old covenant failed not because God’s instruction was faulty but because it was written on stone and the people broke it. The new one will be written inside. Everyone will know the LORD, “from the least to the greatest”, and the reason is the last line of the promise: “For I will forgive their guilt, and I will remember their sin no more.”

No Old Testament passage is quoted at greater length in the New. The letter to the Hebrews sets out the whole of it (8:8–12) and returns to it again (10:16–17). And on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took the cup and called it “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20).

Chapter 32 turns the promise into a deed. With the Babylonian army outside the walls and Jeremiah himself in custody, his cousin Hanamel comes to ask him to buy the family field at Anathoth. Jeremiah buys it, signs the deed before witnesses and has it sealed in a clay jar to last, because God has said, “People will once more buy houses, fields and vineyards in this land.” Then he prays, a little uncertainly: “There is nothing too hard for you.” And God answers him with his own words turned into a question: “Is there anything too hard for me?”

The scroll, the cistern and the fall

The last part of the book tells the story of Jeremiah’s sufferings with a plainness that makes it hard to read. In chapter 36 King Jehoiakim sits by the fire in his winter house while the scroll of Jeremiah’s words is read to him, cutting off each few columns with a knife and throwing them into the fire. Jeremiah simply dictates it again, “and many other words like them were added”.

Under Zedekiah he is beaten, imprisoned, and at last lowered by ropes into a cistern where “there was no water in the cistern, only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud.” He is rescued by a foreigner, Ebed-melech the Cushite, an official of the palace, who lets down old rags for him to put under his arms so the ropes will not cut him. Zedekiah sends for the prophet in secret, again and again, to ask whether there is any word from the LORD. There is, and it does not change.

Then the wall is breached. Zedekiah is caught fleeing, sees his sons killed and is blinded; the city is burned. Jeremiah is freed by the Babylonians and stays with the remnant under the governor Gedaliah, until Gedaliah is murdered and the survivors, against Jeremiah’s pleading, flee to Egypt and take him with them (40–44). There, among the Judeans scattered through Egypt, his last recorded words are a protest against their worship of “the queen of heaven”. We do not know how he died.

A short chapter is addressed to Baruch, who has been complaining of his own sorrows: “Are you seeking great things for yourself? Do not seek them.” He is promised his life, and only that. Then come the oracles against the nations, ending with the longest of all, against Babylon, the empire that had seemed to hold the world. “Here the words of Jeremiah end.”

How to read Jeremiah

Jeremiah is long and not in order, and it is best not to expect to read it like a story. Read the call (1), the temple sermon (7 and 26), the confessions (11–20), the letter to the exiles (29), the Book of Consolation (30–33) and the narrative of the end (36–45) first, and the rest will begin to make sense around them.

Keep the history beside you: Josiah, Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin, Zedekiah, and the three blows of 605, 597 and 587. Many chapters begin by naming the king, and knowing who is on the throne tells you what Jeremiah is facing.

Notice how much the book is about speaking and hearing. Words are put in the prophet’s mouth, eaten as food (15:16), burned and rewritten. God’s word is “like fire” and “like a hammer that smashes rock to pieces”. False prophets say what people want; the true one is known when his word comes to pass. And listen, as you read, for Jeremiah’s tears, because they are God’s too. Again and again it is hard to tell whether it is the prophet or the LORD who is grieving: “If only my head were all water and my eyes a fountain of tears.”

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Much of Jeremiah is poetry, and the poetry is printed one line per line, as it is laid out in the Hebrew. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”. Where the Hebrew has “Lord” and the name together, as in Jeremiah’s first protest, it reads “Lord GOD”.

“The LORD of Armies.” Jeremiah’s favourite title for God, traditionally “the LORD of hosts”, is rendered “the LORD of Armies”: the God who commands the armies of heaven, and before whom Babylon’s army is only a tool.

“Declares the LORD.” The phrase that punctuates almost every oracle, older Bibles’ “saith the LORD”, is printed as “declares the LORD”, marking the prophet’s words as God’s own.

“Loyal love.” The Hebrew hesed, God’s faithful covenant love, is “loyal love”: “I have loved you with an everlasting love, so I have kept on showing you loyal love.”

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Jeremiah 1
fields.body_html:
The words of Jeremiah

1The words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests at Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin, 2to whom the word of the LORD came during the reign of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of Josiah’s reign, 3and it came during the reign of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the end of the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah son of Josiah, king of Judah, the year Jerusalem went into exile, in the fifth month.

Jeremiah is called to be a prophet

4The word of the LORD came to me:
5“I knew you before I shaped you in the womb;
I set you apart before you came out of the womb;
I have given you to the nations as a prophet.”
6I said, “Oh, Lord GOD! I do not know how to speak; I am a mere youth.”

7But the LORD said to me, “Do not say, ‘I am a mere youth.’ To all the people I send you to, you will go; every word I command you, you will speak. 8Have no fear of them, for I am with you to rescue you, declares the LORD.” 9The LORD then stretched out his hand and laid it on my mouth, and the LORD said to me, “There: I have placed my words in your mouth.
10See, on this day I have set you over nations and over kingdoms,
to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and overthrow,
to build and plant.”

An almond rod and a boiling pot

11The word of the LORD came to me: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” I said, “I see a rod cut from an almond tree.” 12The LORD said to me, “You have seen rightly, for I am keeping watch over my word until I carry it out.”

13The word of the LORD came to me a second time: “What do you see?” I said, “I see a pot fanned to a boil, its mouth tilted from the north toward the south.” 14Then the LORD said to me, “From the north, disaster will burst out upon everyone who lives in the land.
15For I am about to summon all the clans of the northern kingdoms, declares the LORD.
They will come, and each of them will set up his throne at the entrance of Jerusalem’s gates, against all its surrounding walls,
and against all the towns of Judah.
16I will pronounce my sentence on them for all their wickedness,
because they have abandoned me, burned offerings to other gods, and bowed down to what their own hands have made.
17As for you, tuck your robe into your belt, get up, and tell them everything I command you.
Do not be shattered by them, or I will shatter you in front of them.
18And I, for my part, have made you today a walled city, a pillar of iron, and walls of bronze, set against the whole land:
against Judah’s kings and officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
19They will make war on you, but they will not overcome you,
for I am with you, declares the LORD, to rescue you.”
fields.summary: God calls Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations, saying he was chosen before he was born, and touches his mouth to give him God’s words. Visions of an almond branch and a boiling pot announce that disaster is coming from the north.

fields.title: Jeremiah 2
fields.body_html:
The devotion of Israel’s youth

1The word of the LORD came to me:
2Go and call out so that Jerusalem hears: The LORD says this:
I remember the loyal love of your youth,
how you loved me as a bride,
how you went after me through the wilderness,
through a land where nothing was sown.
3Israel was set apart as holy to the LORD,
the first share of his harvest.
Whoever ate of it was held guilty,
and disaster came on them, declares the LORD.

Forsaking the spring of living water

4Hear the word of the LORD, house of Jacob,
all you clans of the house of Israel.
5The LORD says this: What did your ancestors find wrong in me,
that they went so far from me,
and went after worthless idols and became worthless themselves?
6They did not ask, “Where is the LORD,
the one who brought us up from Egypt’s land,
who guided us in the wilderness,
through a land of desert plains and pits,
a land of drought and deep darkness,
a land no one crosses and no one lives in?”
7I brought you into orchard land,
to eat its fruit and its good things.
But you came in and defiled my land;
you made my inheritance something detestable.
8The priests did not ask, “Where is the LORD?”
Those who handle the instruction did not know me;
the shepherds rebelled against me;
the prophets prophesied by Baal
and followed things that are of no profit.
9So I will go on bringing charges against you, declares the LORD,
and I will bring charges against your children’s children.
10Go over to the coastlands of Kittim and look;
send to Kedar and think it through with care;
see whether anything like this has ever happened.
11Has any nation ever exchanged its gods,
even though they are not gods at all?
Yet my people have exchanged their glory for something that gives no help.
12Be horrified at this, you heavens;
shudder and be utterly stunned, declares the LORD.
13For my people have committed two evils:
they have abandoned me, the spring of living water,
and cut out cisterns for themselves,
cracked cisterns that can hold no water.
14Is Israel a slave?
Was he born a slave in his master’s house?
Then why has he become plunder?
15Young lions have roared against him;
they have raised their voices.
They have made his land a ruin;
his towns are burned, with no one living there.
16Even the people of Memphis and Tahpanhes
are stripping the crown of your head bare.
17Is this not what you have done to yourself
in forsaking the LORD your God
while he was leading you on the way?
18So now, what do you gain by taking the road to Egypt
to drink the waters of the Shihor?
What do you gain by taking the road to Assyria
to drink the waters of the Euphrates?
19Your own wickedness will punish you, and your turning away will convict you.
Know, then, and see what an evil and bitter thing it is
for you to forsake the LORD your God,
with no dread of me in you,
declares the Lord GOD of Armies.
20Long ago I broke your yoke and tore off your chains,
and you said, “I will not transgress.”
Yet on every high hill and under every leafy tree
you sprawled like a prostitute.
21I planted you as a choice vine,
from seed that was wholly true.
How then have you turned, before me,
into the wild shoots of a strange vine?
22Even if you scrub yourself with washing soda
and use soap in plenty,
your guilt remains a stain before me,
declares the Lord GOD.
23How can you say, “I have not made myself unclean, I have not gone after the Baals”?
Look at your path in the valley;
admit what you have done,
you restless young she-camel, running this way and that!
24A wild donkey at home in the wilderness sniffs the wind in her longing.
In her season of heat, who can turn her back?
The males that seek her need not tire themselves;
at mating time they will find her.
25Do not run until your feet are bare
and your throat is dry with thirst.
But you said, “It is no use!
No, I love strangers,
and I will go after them.”
26As a thief is shamed when he is found out,
so the house of Israel is put to shame:
they, their kings and their officials,
their priests and their prophets,
27who call a tree “My father” and tell a stone, “You gave birth to us.”
They have turned their backs to me, not their faces;
yet when trouble comes they say,
“Rise up and save us!”
28Where then are the gods you made for yourself?
Let them get up, if they can save you
when trouble comes to you.
For you have as many gods
as you have towns, Judah.

Why bring charges against me?

29Why do you bring charges against me?
You have all rebelled against me, declares the LORD.
30It was no use that I struck your children;
they would not accept discipline.
Your own sword devoured your prophets like a ravaging lion.
31And you, this generation, pay heed to the word of the LORD:
Have I been a desert to Israel,
or a land of deep gloom?
Why then do my people say, “We wander where we please;
we will not come back to you”?
32Would a young woman forget her jewels,
a bride the sash she wears?
Yet my people have forgotten me
days beyond counting.
33How skillfully you find your way to look for love!
So you have even taught your ways
to wicked women.
34Even on the hems of your clothes is found
the lifeblood of the innocent poor.
You did not catch them breaking in. Yet in spite of all this,
35you said, “I am guiltless;
his anger has surely left me.”
Now I will bring you to judgment
because you say, “I have not sinned.”
36How lightly you go about changing your course!
You will be put to shame by Egypt too,
just as you were put to shame by Assyria.
37You will come away from Egypt too
with your hands on your head,
because the LORD has rejected the ones you rely on,
and you will not succeed with their help.
fields.summary: God remembers Israel’s early devotion, but the people have exchanged God, the spring of living water, for cracked cisterns and turned to other gods.

fields.title: Jeremiah 3
fields.body_html:
Can a divorced wife come back?

1This is the message: If a man divorces his wife, and she leaves him and marries another man, will he go back to her again?
Would that land not be thoroughly defiled?
Yet you have prostituted yourself with many lovers,
and would you now come back to me? declares the LORD.
2Look up at the bare hilltops and see:
is there any place where you have not been lain with?
You sat by the roadsides waiting for lovers, like a nomad in the desert,
and you have defiled the land with your prostitution and your wickedness.
3So the showers have been held back,
and the spring rain has not come.
Yet your face is as brazen as a prostitute’s;
you will not let yourself feel shame.
4Have you not just now been calling to me, “My father,
you have been my close friend since I was young!
5Will he stay angry forever?
Will he hold on to it to the end?”
That is how you talk, but you do every evil thing you can.

Faithless Israel and treacherous Judah

6The LORD spoke to me during the reign of King Josiah: “Have you seen what faithless Israel did? She went up onto every high hill and under every green tree, and there she prostituted herself. 7I thought, ‘After she has done all this, she will come back to me.’ But she did not come back, and her treacherous sister Judah saw it. 8I saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I sent her away and gave her a certificate of divorce. Yet her treacherous sister Judah was not afraid. She too went and prostituted herself. 9Because her prostitution meant so little to her, she defiled the land, committing adultery with stone and wood. 10Even after all this, her treacherous sister Judah did not come back to me wholeheartedly; it was only a pretense, declares the LORD.”

Return, faithless people

11The LORD said to me, “Faithless Israel has shown herself less guilty than treacherous Judah. 12Go and proclaim this message toward the north: ‘Return, faithless Israel, declares the LORD. I will not look on you in anger, for I am loyal in love, declares the LORD. I will not stay angry forever. 13Only admit your guilt: you have rebelled against the LORD your God, you have run here and there to foreign gods under every green tree, and you have not obeyed my voice, declares the LORD. 14Return, faithless children, declares the LORD, for I am your husband. I will take you, one from a town and two from a clan, and bring you to Zion. 15I will give you shepherds who are after my own heart, and they will shepherd you with knowledge and insight. 16In those days, when you have multiplied and been fruitful in the land, declares the LORD, people will no longer speak of “the ark of the covenant of the LORD.” It will not come to mind; they will not remember it or miss it, and another will not be made. 17At that time Jerusalem will be named the LORD’s throne, and all the nations will gather in Jerusalem to honor the LORD’s name. No longer will they follow the stubbornness of their evil hearts.

18In those days the people of Judah will join the people of Israel, and together they will come from the land of the north to the land I gave your ancestors as their inheritance.’”
19I myself thought, “How I would love to treat you as one of my sons
and give you a pleasant land,
the most beautiful inheritance among the nations!”
I thought you would call me “My father”
and would never turn away from following me.
20But as an unfaithful wife leaves her husband,
so you have been unfaithful to me, house of Israel, declares the LORD.
21A cry is heard on the bare hilltops,
the Israelites weeping and pleading,
because they have twisted their path
and forgotten the LORD their God.
22Return, faithless children,
and I will heal your faithlessness.
“We are here; we have come to you,
because you are the LORD our God.
23Surely the hills are a delusion, and the uproar on the mountains;
surely in the LORD our God
is the salvation of Israel.
24From our youth the shameful god has devoured all that our ancestors worked for:
their flocks and their herds,
their sons and their daughters.
25Let us lie down in our shame and let our disgrace cover us.
For both we and our ancestors have sinned against the LORD our God,
from our youth until this very day,
and we have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God.”
fields.summary: Judah is like an unfaithful wife, worse than her sister Israel. God calls them to return and promises shepherds after God’s own heart.

fields.title: Jeremiah 4
fields.body_html:
If you return, Israel

1If you return, Israel, declares the LORD,
return to me. If you put your detestable idols out of my sight and no longer stray,
2and swear, “As surely as the LORD lives,”
in truth, with justice and with righteousness,
then the nations will bless themselves by him and take pride in him.

Plow up your unplowed ground

3For the LORD says this to the people of Judah and to Jerusalem:
Plow up your unplowed ground,
and do not sow among thorns.
4Circumcise yourselves for the LORD; circumcise your hearts,
people of Judah and people of Jerusalem,
or my wrath will flare up like fire and burn, and no one will put it out,
because of the evil you have done.
5Announce it in Judah, proclaim it in Jerusalem, and say,
“Blow the ram’s horn throughout the land!”
Shout at the top of your voice and say,
“Gather together! Let us go into the fortified cities!”
6Raise a signal flag toward Zion!
Run for safety; do not wait!
For I am bringing disaster from the north, a great and crushing ruin.
7A lion has left his thicket;
a destroyer of nations has broken camp.
He has left his place
to make your land a wasteland.
Your towns will lie in ruins, with no one living in them.
8So dress in sackcloth, lament and wail,
for the LORD’s fierce anger has still not turned away from us.

9On that day, declares the LORD,
the king and the officials will lose heart;
the priests will be horrified,
and the prophets will be stunned.
10Then I said, “Oh, Lord GOD, truly you have led this people and Jerusalem far astray with the words,
‘You will have peace,’
while the sword is pressing at their throats!”
11At that time this people and Jerusalem will be told:
“A scorching wind off the bare hills in the desert
is blowing toward my dear people,
not to winnow and not to clean the grain;
12a wind too strong for that comes at my command.
Now I, too, will pronounce judgment on them.”
13See, he rises like gathering clouds, his chariots like a storm wind;
his horses are quicker than eagles.
“Woe to us! We are ruined!”
14Jerusalem, wash the evil from your heart,
so that you may be saved.
How long will you let your wicked schemes make their home in you?
15For a voice is announcing from Dan,
proclaiming disaster from the hill country of Ephraim.
16Report to the nations: look! Announce it against Jerusalem:
“Besiegers are coming from a far country;
they shout their war cry against the towns of Judah.”
17Like watchmen guarding a field they surround her,
because she has rebelled against me, declares the LORD.
18Your conduct and your deeds
have brought this on you.
This is what your evil brings: how bitter it is,
how it pierces to your heart!

Anguish at the sound of war

19My insides, my insides! I twist in pain! My chest is bursting! My heart pounds within me; I cannot keep quiet,
for you have heard it, my soul: the sound of the ram’s horn,
the battle cry of war.
20Word comes of ruin upon ruin;
the whole land lies devastated.
Without warning my tents are torn down,
my curtains in an instant.
21How long must I look at the signal flag
and listen to the ram’s horn?

22For my people are fools; they do not know me.
They are senseless children;
they have no understanding.
They are skilled at doing evil,
but they do not know how to do good.
23I looked at the earth, and it was without form and empty;
I looked to the heavens, and their light was gone.
24I looked at the mountains, and they were quaking;
all the hills were rocking back and forth.
25I looked, and there was no one at all;
every bird in the sky had flown away.
26I looked, and the orchard land had become a desert;
all its towns had been torn down before the LORD,
before his fierce anger.

27For the LORD says this:
The whole land will be laid waste,
but I will not destroy it completely.
28For this the earth will mourn,
and the sky above will turn dark,
because I have spoken and I have decided;
I have not changed my mind, and I will not turn back from it.
29At the sound of horsemen and archers
the people of every town run away.
They go into the thickets; they climb up among the rocks.
Every town is abandoned;
no one lives in them.
30And you, ruined one, what will you do? Though you dress in scarlet, though you put on jewelry of gold, though you make your eyes look large with paint,
you make yourself beautiful for nothing.
Your lovers reject you; they are out to take your life.
31I hear a scream like that of a woman in labor, the agony of one bearing her first child:
it is the voice of Daughter Zion, fighting for breath and holding out her hands:
“Woe is me!
My life is ebbing away before killers!”
fields.summary: God calls Judah to break up the unplowed ground and circumcise their hearts. A destroyer is coming from the north, and Jeremiah is anguished at the vision of the land laid waste.

fields.title: Jeremiah 5
fields.body_html:
Search for one who acts justly

1Roam the streets of Jerusalem; look around and take note; search her public squares.
See if you can find a single person,
one who acts justly and seeks to be faithful,
and I will pardon the city.
2Even when they say, “As surely as the LORD lives,”
they are swearing to a lie.
3LORD, do not your eyes look for faithfulness?
You struck them, but they felt no pain;
you crushed them, but they would not accept correction.
They set their faces harder than rock;
they would not turn back.
4I said, “These are only the poor;
they act foolishly because they do not know the way of the LORD,
what their God requires.
5I will go to the great and speak with them;
surely they know the way of the LORD,
what their God requires.”
But they too, one and all, had broken the yoke
and snapped the straps.
6So a lion from the forest will attack them, a wolf from the desert will ravage them,
a leopard lies in wait near their towns;
anyone who goes out will be torn to pieces.
For their rebellions are many,
and they have turned away countless times.
7How can I forgive you for this?
Your children have abandoned me
and sworn by what are no gods at all.
I filled them with food, yet they committed adultery
and crowded into the house of a prostitute.
8They are like well-fed, lusty stallions;
each one neighs for his neighbor’s wife.
9Should I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD.
On a nation such as this
should I not take vengeance?

10Go up through her vineyard rows and ruin them,
but do not destroy her completely.
Cut away her branches;
they do not belong to the LORD.
11For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken faith with me completely, declares the LORD.
12They have told lies about the LORD;
they have said, “He will do nothing!
No harm will come to us;
we will not see sword or famine.
13The prophets are nothing but wind;
the word is not in them.
Let what they threaten happen to them!”

A nation from far away

14Therefore the LORD, the God of Armies, says this:
Because you people have spoken these words,
I am making my words in your mouth a fire,
and this people the wood, and the fire will burn them up.
15House of Israel, I am bringing a nation from far away against you, declares the LORD.
It is a nation that endures, a nation from ancient times,
a nation whose language you do not know;
you will not understand what they say.
16Their quiver is like an open grave;
they are all mighty warriors.
17They will devour your harvest and your food; they will devour your sons and your daughters;
they will devour your flocks and your herds;
they will devour your vines and your fig trees.
With the sword they will break down your fortified towns, the towns you trust in.
18Yet even in those days, declares the LORD,
I will not destroy you completely.
19And when the people ask, “Why has the LORD our God done all this to us?”
you must answer them,
“As you abandoned me and served foreign gods in your own land,
so now you will serve strangers in a land not your own.”

A stubborn and rebellious people

20Announce this to the house of Jacob;
make it heard in Judah:
21Listen to this, you foolish people with no sense,
you who have eyes and do not see,
who have ears and do not hear.
22Do you not fear me? declares the LORD. Will you not tremble in my presence?
I set the sand as the boundary of the sea,
a lasting decree it cannot cross.
Its waters may heave, but they cannot win;
its waves may roar, but they cannot pass beyond it.
23But this people has a stubborn, rebellious heart;
they have turned away and gone off.
24They do not say to themselves, “Let us fear the LORD our God,
who gives the rain in its season, the autumn rain and the spring rain,
and keeps for us the weeks set for the harvest.”
25Your guilt has turned these blessings away;
your sins have kept good things from you.
26For there are wicked people among my people.
They lie in wait like hunters crouching for birds;
they set a deadly trap and catch human beings.
27Like a basket full of birds,
their houses are full of what they gained by deceit.
That is how they have become powerful and rich.
28They have grown fat and sleek; their evil deeds go beyond all limits.
They do not take up the case,
the case of the fatherless, yet they prosper;
they do not defend the rights of the needy.
29Should I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD.
On a nation such as this
should I not take vengeance?

30Something shocking and horrible
has happened in the land:
31The prophets prophesy lies, and the priests rule with the prophets’ backing,
and my people like it this way.
But what will you do when the end comes?
fields.summary: No one in Jerusalem does justice or seeks the truth; prophets prophesy lies and the people love it, so a nation from far away will come against them.

fields.title: Jeremiah 6
fields.body_html:
Flee from Jerusalem

1Run for safety, people of Benjamin, out from the middle of Jerusalem!
Sound the ram’s horn in Tekoa,
lift up a signal fire over Beth-haccherem!
For disaster is looming out of the north, a great collapse.
2The lovely and pampered one,
Daughter Zion, I will destroy.
3Shepherds will come against her with their flocks;
they will set up tents on every side of her,
and each will graze his own patch.
4“Make ready a holy war against her!
Up, let us attack at noon!”
“Woe to us! The day is fading,
and the evening shadows are growing long!
5Up, let us attack by night
and destroy her strongholds!”

6For the LORD of Armies says this:
Cut down her trees
and heap up a siege ramp against Jerusalem.
This is the city marked for punishment;
inside her is oppression and nothing else.
7As a well keeps its water fresh,
so she keeps her wickedness flowing.
Violence and ruin echo in her streets; sickness and wounds are always before me.
8Take correction, Jerusalem,
or I will turn from you in disgust,
and make you a wasteland,
a land where no one lives.

9The LORD of Armies says this:
They will glean the remnant of Israel as bare as a vine.
Reach out your hand again like one picking grapes,
over the branches.
10Who is there for me to speak to and warn, so that they will listen?
Their ears are uncircumcised;
they cannot pay attention.
The word of the LORD has become something they mock; they take no pleasure in it.
11But I am filled with the fury of the LORD; I am worn out from holding it back.
Pour it out on the little ones in the street
and on the young men where they gather;
for husband and wife alike will be captured,
the elderly and those who have lived out their years.
12Their houses will pass to others,
their fields and their wives too;
for I will stretch out my hand against the people of the land, declares the LORD.
13For from the smallest of them to the greatest,
all are out for dishonest gain;
from prophet to priest,
every one of them deals in lies.
14They have treated the fracture of my people as though it were slight,
saying, “Peace, peace,”
when there is no peace.
15Were they ashamed when they did such detestable things?
Not in the least; they have forgotten how to blush.
So they will fall with the fallen;
when I call them to account they will be brought down, says the LORD.

The age-old paths

16The LORD says this: Stand where the roads meet and look around; ask about the age-old paths, which one is the good way,
and walk in it; then you will find rest for your souls.
But they answered, “We will not go that way.”
17I set watchmen over you:
“Listen for the blast of the ram’s horn!”
But they said, “We will not listen.”
18Therefore listen, you nations;
know, you assembly, what will happen to them.
19Listen, earth!
I am about to bring disaster on this people, the fruit of their own plotting,
because they have paid no heed to my words,
and my instruction they have tossed aside.
20What do I care for incense brought from Sheba,
or for fragrant cane from a faraway land?
Your burnt offerings do not win my favor;
your sacrifices give me no pleasure.

21So the LORD says this:
I am about to set obstacles in front of this people,
and they will trip over them, parents and children alike; neighbors and friends will die.

An army from the land of the north

22The LORD says this:
See, an army is coming from the land of the north;
a mighty nation is being roused from the ends of the earth.
23They take hold of bow and spear;
they are cruel and show no mercy.
The noise of them roars like the sea
as they ride on horses,
lined up like a warrior for battle against you, Daughter Zion.
24We have heard the news of them, and our hands hang limp;
distress has gripped us,
pain like a woman in labor.
25Do not go out into the countryside;
do not travel on the roads;
for the enemy’s sword is there,
terror on every side.
26My dear people, put on sackcloth
and roll in the ashes;
mourn as for an only son,
with the bitterest wailing;
for suddenly the destroyer will fall on us.
27I have made you a tester of metals among my people, strong as a fortress,
so that you may learn and test their ways.
28They are all hardened rebels,
going around spreading slander. They are bronze and iron;
every one of them is corrupt.
29The bellows blast away,
the lead is burned up in the fire,
but the refining goes on for nothing;
the wicked are not drawn off.
30They are called worthless silver,
because the LORD has thrown them away.
fields.summary: Jerusalem will be besieged because it is full of oppression. The people say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace, and they refuse to walk in the ancient paths.

fields.title: Jeremiah 7
fields.body_html:
The message at the temple gate

1This message came to Jeremiah from the LORD: 2“Take your stand at the gate of the house of the LORD and announce this word there. Say: ‘Hear the word of the LORD, all Judah, everyone who comes in through these gates to worship the LORD.

3The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Change your ways and your actions for the better, and I will let you live in this place. 4Do not trust in deceptive words when people say, “This is the LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple, the LORD’s temple!” 5If you really change your ways and your actions for the better, if you truly treat one another with justice, 6if you do not oppress the outsider, the fatherless child and the widow, and do not shed innocent blood in this place, and do not follow other gods to your own ruin, 7then I will let you go on living here in this place, in the land I gave your ancestors long ago, for all time. 8But look, you are trusting in deceptive words that are worthless. 9Will you steal and murder and commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods you have never known, 10and then come and stand before me in this house that bears my name and say, “We are safe!”, only to go on doing all these detestable things? 11Has this house that bears my name become a hideout for robbers in your eyes? I myself have seen it, declares the LORD.

12Go now to my place in Shiloh, where I first made my name dwell, and look at what I did to it on account of the wickedness of my people Israel. 13And now, declares the LORD, because you have done all these things, and I spoke to you again and again and you would not listen, and I called you and you did not answer, 14so I will do to this house that bears my name, the house you trust in, and to the place I gave you and your ancestors, what I did to Shiloh. 15I will throw you out of my presence, just as I threw out all your kin, all the descendants of Ephraim.’

16As for you, do not pray for this people. Do not raise a cry or a prayer for them, and do not plead with me, because I will not listen to you. 17Do you not see what they are doing in the towns of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? 18The children gather wood, the fathers light the fire, and the women knead dough to make cakes for the queen of heaven. They pour drink offerings out to other gods, and so they provoke me to anger. 19Is it really me they are provoking? declares the LORD. Is it not themselves they hurt, to their own disgrace?

20So the Lord GOD says this: Look, my anger, my fury, is about to be poured out on this place, on people and animals, on the trees of the field and the crops of the ground. It will burn and not be put out.

Obey my voice

21The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Go ahead, add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the meat yourselves! 22For when I brought your ancestors out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to them or give them commands about burnt offerings and sacrifices. 23Instead, this is what I commanded them: ‘Obey my voice; then I will be your God, and you will be my people. Walk in every way I command you, so that it may go well with you.’ 24But they did not listen or pay attention. They followed their own plans, in the stubbornness of their evil hearts. They went backward instead of forward. 25From the day your ancestors left the land of Egypt until today, I have sent you all my servants the prophets, day after day, again and again. 26Yet they did not listen to me or pay attention. They stiffened their necks and did more evil than their ancestors. 27When you speak all these words to them, they will not listen to you; when you call them, they will give you no answer. 28Then say to them, ‘This is the nation that has not obeyed the LORD its God and would not accept correction. Faithfulness has died; it is gone from their lips.’

The Valley of Slaughter

29Cut off your consecrated hair and throw it away; raise a lament on the bare hills, for the LORD has rejected and abandoned the generation that is under his wrath. 30The people of Judah have done what is evil in my sight, declares the LORD. They have placed their detestable idols in the house that bears my name and so defiled it. 31In the Valley of Ben-hinnom they have built the high places of Topheth, to burn their sons and daughters in the fire, a thing I never commanded and that never entered my mind.

32So look, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when it will no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter. They will bury the dead in Topheth because there will be no room anywhere else. 33The dead bodies of this people will become food for the birds of the sky and for the wild animals, and no one will scare them off. 34In the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem I will silence the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of bridegroom and bride, for the land will lie in ruins.
fields.summary: At the temple gate Jeremiah warns the people not to trust in the words “the temple of God” while they oppress the weak and follow other gods. God will do to the temple what was done to Shiloh.

fields.title: Jeremiah 8
fields.body_html:
1At that time, declares the LORD, the bones of Judah’s kings and officials, of the priests and prophets, and of all who lived in Jerusalem will be taken from their graves. 2They will lie spread out under the sun, the moon and the whole host of heaven, which they loved and served, which they followed, consulted and worshiped. No one will gather them or bury them; they will lie like dung on the surface of the ground. 3All who are left of this evil family, in every place where I have driven them, will choose death rather than life, declares the LORD of Armies.”

A people who will not turn back

4Say to them, The LORD says this:
When people fall, do they not get up again?
When someone turns away, do they not turn back?
5Why then has this people, Jerusalem, turned away, and kept on turning away?
They cling to deceit;
they refuse to come back.
6I have listened closely and heard; they do not speak what is right.
No one is sorry for their wickedness
and says, “What have I done?”
Each of them turns off on their own course,
like a horse charging into battle.
7Even the stork in the sky knows her seasons,
and the turtledove, the swift and the crane keep the time of their return;
but my people do not know
the order the LORD has set.
8How can you say, “We are wise;
we have the instruction of the LORD”?
In fact, the lying pen of the scribes
has turned it into a lie.
9The wise will be put to shame;
they will be shattered and trapped.
They have rejected the word of the LORD,
so what kind of wisdom do they have?

10So I will give their wives to others and their fields to conquerors;
for from the smallest to the greatest,
all are out for dishonest gain;
from prophet to priest,
every one of them deals in lies.
11They have treated the fracture of my dear people as though it were slight,
saying, “Peace, peace,”
when there is no peace.
12Were they ashamed when they did such detestable things?
Not in the least; they have forgotten how to blush.
So they will fall with the fallen;
when the time comes to call them to account they will be brought down, says the LORD.

13I will gather them in and put an end to them, declares the LORD.
There are no grapes on the vine, no figs on the fig tree; even the leaves have withered.
What I gave them will pass away from them.
14“Why are we sitting here?
Come together, let us go into the fortified cities and meet our end there;
for the LORD our God has doomed us to die and made us drink poisoned water,
because we have sinned against the LORD.
15We hoped for peace, but nothing good came;
for a time of healing, but there was only terror.”
16The snorting of the enemy’s horses is heard from Dan; at the neighing of his stallions
the whole land shakes.
They come and devour the land and all that is in it,
the city with its people.

17For I am about to send snakes among you,
vipers that no charmer can control,
and they will bite you, declares the LORD.

Is there no balm in Gilead?

18My joy is gone; grief has come over me;
my heart is sick within me.
19Listen! The cry of my dear people for help comes from a land far away:
“Is the LORD not in Zion?
Is her King no longer there?”
Why have they made me angry with their idols, with worthless foreign gods?
20“The harvest is over and the summer is gone,
and still we are not saved.”
21Because my dear people are broken, I am broken;
I mourn, and horror has taken hold of me.
22Is there no balm in Gilead?
Is there no doctor there?
Why then has the wound of my dear people
not been healed?
fields.summary: The people hold fast to deceit and do not return. Jeremiah weeps for his people: the harvest is past and they are not saved, and there is no balm in Gilead.

fields.title: Jeremiah 9
fields.body_html:
1If only my head were all water
and my eyes a fountain of tears,
so that I could weep day and night
for the slain of my dear people!
2If only I had a travelers’ shelter in the wilderness,
so that I could leave my people and go far away from them!
For they are all adulterers,
a crowd of traitors.
3They bend their tongues like bows to shoot lies;
they have grown strong in the land, but not by truth.
For they go on from one evil to the next, and they do not know me, declares the LORD.

Do not trust any neighbor

4Be on guard, every one of you, against your neighbor,
and put no trust in any brother.
For every brother is a cheat like Jacob,
and every neighbor goes around spreading slander.
5Everyone cheats their neighbor,
and no one speaks the truth.
They have trained their tongues to tell lies; they wear themselves out doing wrong.
6You live surrounded by deceit;
in their deceit they refuse to know me, declares the LORD.

7Therefore the LORD of Armies says this:
I am going to refine them and put them to the test,
for how else can I deal with my dear people?
8Their tongue is a sharpened arrow; it speaks deceit.
With their mouths they speak peace to their neighbors,
but in their hearts they set an ambush for them.
9Should I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD.
On a nation such as this
should I not take vengeance?

10I will weep and wail for the mountains, and raise a lament for the pastures in the wilderness,
because they are scorched and no one travels through them,
and no one hears the lowing of cattle.
The birds of the sky and the animals
have all fled and are gone.
11I will turn Jerusalem into a heap of ruins, a den for jackals,
and I will make the towns of Judah a wasteland where no one lives.

12Who is wise enough to understand this?
To whom has the LORD spoken, so that they can explain it?
Why has the land been ruined
and laid waste like a wilderness that no one crosses?

13And the LORD answered:
It is because they have abandoned my instruction, which I set before them;
they have not obeyed my voice or followed it,
14but have followed the stubbornness of their own hearts
and gone after the Baals, as their ancestors taught them.

15Therefore the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says this:
I am going to feed this people bitter wormwood
and give them poisoned water to drink.
16I will scatter them among nations that neither they nor their ancestors have known,
and I will send the sword to pursue them until I have finished them off.

Call for the mourning women

17The LORD of Armies says this:
Think about what is happening, and call for the mourning women; let them come.
Send for the women who are skilled in lament; let them come,
18and let them hurry and raise a wailing over us,
so that our eyes overflow with tears
and water streams from our eyelids.
19For the sound of wailing is heard from Zion: “How we are ruined!
How deep is our shame! We have had to leave the land,
because our homes have been torn down.”

20Now, you women, listen to the word of the LORD;
let your ears take in the word from his mouth.
Teach your daughters a song of mourning,
and teach one another a lament.
21For death has climbed in through our windows
and entered our strongholds,
to cut off the children from the streets
and the young men from the public squares.
22Say this, declares the LORD:
Human corpses will fall like dung on the open field,
like cut grain left behind the reaper, with no one to gather them.

Let the one who boasts boast in this

23The LORD says this: The wise must not boast about their wisdom, the strong must not boast about their strength, and the rich must not boast about their wealth. 24Instead, whoever boasts should boast of this: that they understand and know me, that I am the LORD, who acts with loyal love, justice and righteousness on the earth. For these are what I delight in, declares the LORD.

25The time is coming, declares the LORD, when I will bring punishment on all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised, 26Egypt, Judah, Edom, the Ammonites, Moab, and all who clip the hair at their temples and live in the desert. For every one of these nations is uncircumcised, and the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.
fields.summary: Jeremiah wishes his eyes were a fountain of tears for his people. No one should boast of wisdom or strength, but only of knowing God, who delights in loyal love, justice and righteousness.

fields.title: Jeremiah 10
fields.body_html:
The idols and the living God

1Hear the word that the LORD has spoken to you, house of Israel.
2The LORD says this: Do not take up the ways of the nations,
and do not be terrified by signs in the sky,
though the nations are terrified by them.
3The customs of the peoples are empty breath:
a tree is cut down from the forest
and worked by a craftsman’s hands with his tool.
4He decorates it with silver and gold;
they fix it in place with hammer and nails so that it will not topple over.
5Like a scarecrow in a cucumber patch, they cannot speak;
they have to be carried, for they cannot walk.
Do not be afraid of them: they can do no harm,
and they have no power to do good either.

6No one is like you, LORD;
you are great, and your name is great in power.
7Who would not fear you, King of the nations?
That is your due.
Among all the wise of the nations and in all their kingdoms there is no one like you.
8They are senseless and foolish, all of them alike;
the teaching of empty idols is only a block of wood.
9Silver hammered into sheets is brought from Tarshish, and gold from Uphaz;
they are the work of a craftsman and the hands of a goldsmith.
Their robes are blue and purple;
every one of them is the work of experts.
10But the LORD is God in truth;
he is the living God, the eternal King.
When he is angry, the earth quakes,
and the nations cannot withstand his fury.

11This is what you are to say to them:
“The gods that did not make heaven and earth
will perish from the earth and from beneath these heavens.”

12It is he who made the earth by his power,
who set the world firm by his wisdom,
and by his understanding spread out the heavens.
13When he thunders, the waters in the heavens roar;
he raises the clouds from the far edges of the earth.
He makes lightning flash with the rain
and brings the wind out of his storehouses.
14Everyone proves senseless and ignorant;
every goldsmith is shamed by his idol,
for the images he casts are a fraud, with no breath in them.
15They are empty breath, a work to be laughed at;
when the time comes to punish them, they will perish.
16The God who is Jacob’s portion is not like these, for he is the one who formed all things,
and Israel is the tribe he holds as his own;
the LORD of Armies is his name.

Pack your bundle for exile

17Pick up your bundle to leave the land,
you who live under siege.

18For the LORD says this:
This time I am about to sling out the people of the land;
I will hem them in so that they feel it.

19Woe is me because of my injury!
My wound is severe.
But I said, “This is truly a sickness, and I must bear it.”
20My tent is destroyed,
and all its ropes are snapped.
My children have gone from me and are no more;
there is no one left to pitch my tent again
or to hang up my curtains.
21For the shepherds have turned senseless
and have not sought the LORD;
so they have had no success,
and all their flock is scattered.

22Listen! A report! Here it comes:
a great rumbling from the land of the north,
to turn the cities of Judah into a wasteland, a haunt of jackals.

A prayer for just correction

23I know, LORD,
that a person’s way is not in their own hands;
no one who walks can set the course of their own steps.
24Correct me, LORD, but in just measure,
not in your anger, or you will bring me to nothing.
25Pour out your fury on the nations that have not known you,
on the peoples
that never call on your name.
For they have swallowed up Jacob, swallowed him and finished him off,
and left his homeland desolate.
fields.summary: Idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field, but God is the true and living God. Jeremiah grieves over the coming exile and prays for correction with justice.

fields.title: Jeremiah 11
fields.body_html:
The words of this covenant

1This message came to Jeremiah from the LORD: 2“Listen to the words of this covenant, and speak them to the people of Judah and to those who live in Jerusalem. 3Say to them, ‘The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: Cursed is anyone who does not obey the words of this covenant, 4which I commanded your ancestors when I brought them from the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace. I told them, “Listen to my voice and carry out these words, doing all that I command you; then you will be my people, and I will be your God,” 5so that I might keep the oath I swore to your ancestors, that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey; and so it is today.’” I answered, “Amen, LORD.”

6Then the LORD said to me, “Announce all these words in the towns of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem: ‘Listen to the words of this covenant and carry them out. 7For I warned your ancestors in the strongest terms when I brought them up from the land of Egypt, and I have warned them again and again until today: “Listen to my voice.” 8But they did not listen or pay attention. Each of them walked in the stubbornness of their evil hearts. So I brought on them all that this covenant threatens, for I had commanded them to keep it, but they did not keep it.’”

9Then the LORD said to me, “A conspiracy has come to light among the people of Judah and among those who live in Jerusalem. 10They have gone back to the sins of their earliest ancestors, who refused to listen to my words; they too have followed other gods and served them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have both broken my covenant, the one I made with their ancestors.

11So the LORD says this: I am about to bring a disaster on them that they will not be able to escape. When they cry out to me, I will not listen to them. 12Then the towns of Judah and those who live in Jerusalem will go and cry out to the gods they burn offerings to, but those gods will never save them when their disaster comes. 13For you have as many gods as you have towns, Judah, and you have set up as many altars to that shameful thing as there are streets in Jerusalem, altars for burning offerings to Baal.

14As for you, do not pray for this people. Do not lift up a cry or a prayer for them, because I will not listen when they call out to me because of their trouble.

15What right does my beloved have in my house, when she has carried out so many evil schemes?
Can sacred meat take your disaster away from you,
so that you could rejoice?
16‘A green olive tree, beautiful with fine fruit’:
that is what the LORD named you.
But with the noise of a great storm he will set it on fire,
and its branches will be broken.
17The LORD of Armies, who planted you, has decreed disaster against you because of the evil the house of Israel and the house of Judah have done to their own harm, provoking me to anger by burning offerings to Baal.”

The men of Anathoth seek Jeremiah’s life

18The LORD let me know, and so I knew;
then you showed me what they were doing.
19I was like a trusting lamb being led away to be slaughtered;
I did not know it was against me that they were making their plans:
“Let us destroy the tree, fruit and all; let us cut him off from the land of the living,
so that his name is never remembered again.”
20But LORD of Armies, you who judge with justice,
who test the inner feelings and the mind,
let me see you take vengeance on them,
for I have laid my case before you.

21So the LORD says this about the men of Anathoth,
who are seeking your life and saying,
“Do not prophesy in the name of the LORD,
if you do not want to die at our hands,”

22the LORD of Armies says this: I am about to punish them.
Their young men will die by the sword,
and their sons and daughters will die by famine,
23and none of them will be left,
for I will bring disaster on the men of Anathoth
in the year of their punishment.
fields.summary: Judah has broken the covenant, so disaster will come. The men of Anathoth plot to kill Jeremiah, and God promises to punish them.

fields.title: Jeremiah 12
fields.body_html:
Why does the way of the wicked succeed?

1You are in the right, LORD, whenever I bring a case against you;
still, I must set my charges before you:
Why does the way of the wicked succeed?
Why do all the faithless live untroubled?
2You planted them, and they have taken root;
they flourish and bear fruit.
You are near in their mouths
but far from their inmost being.
3But you, LORD, know me; you see me
and test how my heart stands toward you.
Drag them away like sheep to be slaughtered;
set them apart for the day of killing.

4How long will the land mourn
and the plants of every field dry up?
Because of the evil of those who live in it,
animals and birds have perished,
for the people say, “He will not see what becomes of us.”
5If you have raced with runners on foot and they have worn you out,
how will you keep pace with horses?
If you feel secure only in a peaceful land,
what will you do in the thick brush along the Jordan?
6Your brothers too, the household of your own father,
even they have broken faith with you;
they too have raised a loud outcry against you.
Do not believe them, though they speak kindly to you.

I have left my house

7I have left my house;
I have cast off my inheritance.
I have handed the one I love with all my heart over to her enemies.
8My inheritance has turned on me like a lion in the forest;
she roars against me, and so I have come to hate her.
9Has my inheritance become to me a speckled bird of prey,
set upon by birds of prey on every side?
Go, gather all the wild animals; bring them to eat.
10Many shepherds have wrecked my vineyard
and trampled down my field;
they have turned the field I delight in into an empty wilderness.
11It has been made a desolation;
ruined, it mourns before me.
The whole land lies desolate,
because no one takes it to heart.
12Destroyers have swept over all the bare hills in the wilderness,
for the sword of the LORD is eating its way from one end of the land to the other;
no living thing has peace.

13They sowed wheat but reaped thorns;
they wore themselves out for nothing.
Be ashamed of your harvests,
because of the fierce anger of the LORD.

Uprooted and brought back

14The LORD says this concerning all my wicked neighbors who lay hands on the inheritance I gave my people Israel to possess: Look, I am going to uproot them from their own soil, and the house of Judah I will uproot from their midst. 15But after I have uprooted them, I will again have compassion on them, and I will bring them back, each one to their own inheritance and each one to their own land. 16And if they will truly learn the ways of my people, swearing by my name, “As surely as the LORD lives,” as they themselves once taught my people to swear by Baal, they will be built up in the midst of my people. 17But if they will not listen, I will uproot that nation, uprooting it and destroying it completely, declares the LORD.
fields.summary: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper, and God answers that worse is coming. God has abandoned the heritage but will have compassion on the nations that learn God’s ways.

fields.title: Jeremiah 13
fields.body_html:
The ruined loincloth

1The LORD said this to me: “Go and buy a linen loincloth and put it on around your waist, but do not put it in water.” 2So I bought the loincloth as the LORD had told me and put it on around my waist.

3The word of the LORD came to me a second time: 4“Take the loincloth you bought, the one you are wearing, and set out for the Euphrates. Hide it there in a crack in the rock.” 5So I went and hid it by the Euphrates, as the LORD had commanded me. 6After many days the LORD said to me, “Set out for the Euphrates and take from there the loincloth I commanded you to hide there.” 7So I went to the Euphrates and dug, and I took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And there it was, ruined, of no use for anything.

8Then the word of the LORD came to me: 9“The LORD says this: This is how I will ruin Judah’s pride, the great pride of Jerusalem. 10This evil people, who refuse to hear my words, who follow the stubbornness of their hearts and have gone after other gods to serve and worship them, will be like this loincloth, of no use for anything. 11For as a loincloth clings to a man’s waist, so I made all the house of Israel and all the house of Judah cling to me, declares the LORD, to be my people and to bring me renown, praise and honor. But they would not listen. 12So say this word to them: ‘The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: Every jar will be filled with wine.’ And they will answer you, ‘Do we not know very well that every jar will be filled with wine?’ 13Then say to them, ‘The LORD says this: I am going to fill everyone who lives in this land with drunkenness: the kings who sit on David’s throne, and the priests, the prophets and all who live in Jerusalem. 14I will smash them against one another, parents and children alike, declares the LORD. I will not pity them or spare them or show them compassion; nothing will keep me from destroying them.’”

Do not be proud

15Listen and pay attention; do not be proud,
for the LORD has spoken.
16Give glory to the LORD your God before he makes it dark,
before your feet stumble on the mountains at dusk.
You will look for light, but he will turn it into deep darkness
and make it black gloom.
17But if you will not listen,
I will weep in hiding over your pride.
My eyes will weep bitterly and overflow with tears,
because the flock of the LORD has been carried off into captivity.

To the king and the queen mother

18Say to the king and to the queen mother, “Step down and sit in a lowly place,
for your splendid crowns have fallen from your heads.”
19The towns of the Negev are shut tight, with no one to open them.
All Judah has been taken into exile, carried away completely.

20Look up and see
the ones coming from the north!
Where is the flock that was entrusted to you,
your fine flock of sheep?
21What will you say when he sets over you as rulers
the very ones you trained to be your close allies?
Will not pains grip you
like a woman in labor?
22And if you ask yourself,
“Why have these things happened to me?”
It is because of your great guilt that your skirts have been lifted and your body treated with violence.
23Can a Cushite change his skin,
or a leopard its spots?
Then you too could do good,
you who have been schooled in evil.
24I will scatter them like chaff
blown off by the desert wind.
25This is your lot, the share I have measured out to you, declares the LORD,
because you have forgotten me
and put your trust in lies.
26So I myself will pull your skirts up over your face,
and your shame will be there for all to see.
27Your adulteries and your lustful neighing,
your shameless prostitution on the hills, out in the open country: I have seen your detestable things.
Woe to you, Jerusalem!
You will not become clean. How much longer will it be?
fields.summary: Jeremiah buries a linen loincloth until it is ruined, a sign of how God will ruin Judah’s pride. Jars filled with wine picture the drunkenness of judgment.

fields.title: Jeremiah 14
fields.body_html:
The drought

1The word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah about the droughts:
2Judah mourns,
her gates droop and fail; her people sit on the ground in black,
and the cry of Jerusalem rises.
3Their nobles send their young servants to fetch water;
they reach the cisterns and there is no water; their vessels come back empty.
They are ashamed and disgraced, and they cover their heads.
4Because of the ground, cracked open
since no rain has come on the land,
the farmers are put to shame; they cover their heads.
5Even the doe in the open field gives birth and then leaves her young behind,
because there is no grass.
6Wild donkeys stand on the bare heights,
gasping for air like jackals;
their eyes grow dim, because there are no plants.
7Even though our sins bear witness against us, LORD,
act for the sake of your name;
for we have turned away many times; we have sinned against you.
8Hope of Israel, who saves it in a time of trouble,
why do you seem an outsider in the land,
a traveler who turns aside to camp for one night?
9Why are you like someone stunned,
like a soldier who cannot save anyone?
Yet you are among us, LORD, and your name is spoken over us; do not abandon us.

10The LORD says this about this people: They love to wander;
they do not keep their feet in check.
So the LORD takes no pleasure in them;
now he will remember their guilt and punish their sins.

Prophets who promise peace

11Then the LORD said to me, “Do not pray for the good of this people. 12When they fast, I will not hear their cry; when they present burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will take no pleasure in them. No, I am going to put an end to them by sword, famine and plague.”

13Then I said, “Oh, Lord GOD! Look, the prophets tell them, ‘The sword you will not see, and famine will not come on you; instead I will give you peace that is sure, here in this place.’”
