Daughter Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time it is stamped down;
in a little while
the time of her harvest will come.
34“Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon has devoured me and crushed me;
he has left me standing like an empty jar.
He has swallowed me like a sea monster,
filled his belly with my good things,
and spewed me out.”
35“May the violence done to me and to my flesh fall on Babylon,”
the people of Zion will say.
“May my blood be on those who live in Chaldea,”
Jerusalem will say.

36Therefore the LORD says this:
I will plead your case
and avenge you.
I will dry up her sea
and leave her spring dry.
37Babylon will become a heap of ruins, a haunt of jackals, a horror and an object of scorn, where no one lives.
38They roar together like young lions;
they growl like lion cubs.
39While they are heated with greed, I will set out a feast for them
and make them drunk, so that they shout and laugh,
and they will sleep a sleep that lasts forever and never wake, declares the LORD.
40I will lead them down like lambs to be slaughtered,
like rams and male goats.
41How Sheshach is taken,
the pride of the whole earth seized!
How Babylon has become a horror among the nations!
42The sea has risen over Babylon;
she is covered by its roaring waves.
43Her towns have become a horror,
a dry land and a desert,
a land where no one lives,
where no human being passes through.
44I will punish Bel in Babylon and make him spit out what he has swallowed.
Nations will stream to him no more;
even Babylon’s wall has fallen.
45Come out of her, my people!
Every one of you, run for your life from the fierce anger of the LORD!
46Do not lose heart or be afraid
at the rumors heard in the land,
one rumor this year, another the next,
rumors of violence in the land and of ruler against ruler.
47Therefore the days are coming
when I will punish Babylon’s idols.
Her whole land will be put to shame,
and all her slain will fall within her.
48Then heaven and earth and everything in them
will sing for joy over Babylon,
for destroyers will come against her from the north, declares the LORD.
49Babylon must fall
because of Israel’s slain,
just as because of Babylon the slain of the whole earth have fallen.
50You who have escaped the sword,
go! Do not linger!
Remember the LORD in that distant land,
and let Jerusalem come to your mind.
51“We are ashamed, for we have heard insults;
disgrace covers our faces,
because foreigners have gone into
the holy places of the LORD’s house.”

52Therefore the days are coming, declares the LORD,
when I will bring punishment on her idols,
and the dying will groan in every part of her land.
53Even if Babylon should climb to the heavens
and make her lofty stronghold secure,
I will send destroyers against her, declares the LORD.

54Listen! A cry rises from Babylon,
the crash of great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!
55For the LORD is destroying Babylon
and silencing her loud noise.
Their waves roar like mighty waters;
the din of their voices rises.
56For a destroyer has come against her, against Babylon.
Her warriors are captured,
their bows are broken,
for the LORD is a God who repays; he will repay in full.
57I will make her officials and wise men drunk, her governors, deputies and warriors,
and they will sleep a sleep that lasts forever and never wake,
declares the King,
whose name is the LORD of Armies.

58The LORD of Armies says this: The broad wall of Babylon will be leveled to the ground,
and her high gates will be set on fire.
The peoples toil for nothing; the nations wear themselves out only for the fire.

Seraiah’s scroll in the Euphrates

59This is the message that Jeremiah the prophet gave as a command to Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, when he went to Babylon with Zedekiah king of Judah in the fourth year of his reign. Seraiah was the quartermaster. 60Jeremiah had written on a single scroll all the disaster that would come on Babylon, all these words written about Babylon. 61Jeremiah said to Seraiah, “When you reach Babylon, see that you read all these words aloud, 62and say, ‘LORD, you have said that you will destroy this place, so that nothing will live in it, neither people nor animals, and it will be a desolation forever.’ 63When you have finished reading this scroll, tie a stone to it and throw it into the middle of the Euphrates, 64and say, ‘So Babylon will sink and rise no more, because of the disaster I am bringing on her, and they will grow weary.’” Here the words of Jeremiah end.
fields.summary: God will bring destruction on Babylon and will repay her for what she did to Zion. Jeremiah’s words are written on a scroll and sunk in the Euphrates.

fields.title: Jeremiah 52
fields.body_html:
Jerusalem falls to Babylon

1Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah. 2He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, as Jehoiakim had done. 3It was because of the anger of the LORD that all this happened in Jerusalem and Judah, until he cast them out of his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. 4On the tenth day of the tenth month, in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon advanced on Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped against the city and built siege works against it on every side. 5The city was under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. 6By the ninth day of the fourth month the city was gripped by famine, and the people of the land had no food. 7Then the city wall was breached, and all the soldiers fled. They left the city by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, though the Chaldeans were all around the city, and they went off toward the Arabah. 8But the Chaldean army chased the king and caught up with Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army scattered away from him. 9They seized the king and took him up to Riblah in the land of Hamath, to the king of Babylon, and there the king passed sentence on him. 10The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons while he watched, and he also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah. 11Then he put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in bronze fetters, and the king of Babylon took him to Babylon and kept him in prison until the day he died. 12In the fifth month, on the tenth day, the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadrezzar’s reign over Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, who served the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem. 13He burned the house of the LORD, the king’s palace and all the houses of Jerusalem; every important house he burned down. 14The whole Chaldean army that was with the captain of the guard tore down all the walls around Jerusalem. 15Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile some of the poorest of the people, the rest of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen. 16But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest people of the land to tend the vineyards and work the fields. 17The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars that belonged to the house of the LORD, the stands, and the bronze Sea that was in the house of the LORD, and they hauled all the metal off to Babylon. 18They also took away the pots, the shovels, the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the dishes and all the bronze utensils used in the temple service. 19The captain of the guard took away the cups, the firepans, the sprinkling bowls, the pots, the lampstands, the dishes and the jars for drink offerings, everything that was made of gold and everything that was made of silver. 20As for the two pillars, the one Sea and the twelve bronze bulls under the stands, which King Solomon made for the house of the LORD, the bronze of all these things was more than could be weighed. 21As for the pillars, each pillar was about 27 feet high, and it took a line of about 18 feet to go around it. Its metal was about 3 inches thick, and it was hollow. 22On top of it was a bronze capital. The capital was about 7 1/2 feet high, with a network and pomegranates all around it, all of bronze. The second pillar, with its pomegranates, was the same. 23There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides; in all there were a hundred pomegranates on the network all around. 24The captain of the guard also seized Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next to him, and the three doorkeepers. 25From the city he took a court officer who had been in charge of the soldiers, seven of the king’s advisers who were found in the city, the secretary of the commander of the army, who mustered the people of the land for war, and sixty of the people of the land who were still in the city. 26Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard led them away to Riblah and brought them before the king of Babylon. 27The king of Babylon had them struck down and executed at Riblah, in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile, away from its own land. 28These are the people Nebuchadrezzar carried into exile: in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans. 29In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar, 832 people from Jerusalem. 30In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile 745 Judeans. In all there were 4,600 people.

Kindness to Jehoiachin

31In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah went into exile, on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach king of Babylon, in the year he became king, showed favor to Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison. 32He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon. 33So Jehoiachin put off his prison clothes, and for the rest of his life he ate regularly at the king’s table. 34And the king of Babylon gave him a regular allowance, a portion for each day, until the day he died, all the days of his life.
fields.summary: Babylon besieges Jerusalem, Zedekiah is captured and the temple is burned. The exiles are counted, and in Babylon King Jehoiachin is released from prison.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
And the king of Babylon gave him a regular allowance, a portion for each day, until the day he died, all the days of his life.

— Jeremiah 52:34

Jeremiah ends quietly, far from the prophet himself. Jerusalem is ashes, its people scattered, and Jehoiachin, the king of David’s line carried off before the end, has spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison. Then a new king of Babylon lets him out, gives him a seat at his table and a portion for each day. It is only a thread, and the thread is still attached to David.

The question the book leaves with you

Jeremiah spent forty years telling people what they did not want to hear, and almost nobody listened. He was mocked, beaten, put in the stocks, thrown into a cistern and carried off to Egypt against his will. By any ordinary measure his ministry failed. And yet his words outlived the king who burned them.

So the book asks every reader the question Jeremiah asked at the crossroads: “ask about the age-old paths, which one is the good way, and walk in it; then you will find rest for your souls.” His hearers answered, “We will not go that way.” The book is honest about how hard it is to hear God’s word when it goes against everything we have planned. It is just as honest about the alternative. The people who trusted the temple, the alliances and the comforting prophets lost all of them. The prophet who trusted God lost nearly everything else, and kept God.

And the book asks what we will do with a God who grieves. Jeremiah’s tears and God’s are hard to tell apart. Judgement in this book is never cold. It is the sorrow of a husband betrayed and a father whose heart aches for his son, and it is always followed by “Return”.

Where the book points

Jeremiah does not end with the exile; it ends with promises that reach far beyond it. He spoke of a “righteous Branch for David” who would “do justice and righteousness in the land”, and whose name would be “The LORD Is Our Righteousness.” He spoke of a covenant written on the heart and of sins remembered no more. He said the seventy years would end, and a generation later Daniel, reading his book in Babylon, counted the years and prayed.

The New Testament hears Jeremiah everywhere. When Jesus asked who people said he was, some answered, “Jeremiah or another of the prophets.” He wept over Jerusalem as Jeremiah had, and quoted Jeremiah’s temple sermon as he cleansed the temple. At the Last Supper he gave his disciples the cup of “the new covenant in my blood”. And the letter to the Hebrews quotes the new covenant promise in full, and concludes that by calling it new, God has treated the first as old, and what grows old is “close to vanishing.” What Jeremiah could only promise, the church believes Christ has brought: forgiveness, and God’s law written on the heart by his Spirit.

Where to go from here

Some of the best preaching on Jeremiah is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the new covenant (Jeremiah 31–32). Andrew Murray’s The Two Covenants, whose chapters on the new covenant and the everlasting covenant are expositions of Jeremiah 31:31–34 and 32:38–40.
  • On the prophet’s call (Jeremiah 1). John Henry Newman’s sermon Jeremiah, a Lesson for the Disappointed (Jeremiah 1:8), and A. B. Simpson’s chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Life and Testimony of Jeremiah” in The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, Part I.
  • On false peace and the old paths (Jeremiah 6). George Whitefield’s The Method of Grace (6:14); J. C. Ryle’s chapter “The Good Way” in The Upper Room and Newman’s “Stedfastness in the Old Paths” in Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume VII, both on 6:16.
  • On the heart (Jeremiah 17). John Wesley’s sermon “The Deceitfulness of the Human Heart” (17:9), in his Sermons on Several Occasions.
  • On the potter and the Branch (Jeremiah 18 and 23). Whitefield’s “The Potter and the Clay” (18:1–6), in Selected Sermons of George Whitefield, and his sermon The Lord Our Righteousness (23:6).
  • On prayer and the word (Jeremiah 14, 15 and 33). Robert Murray M’Cheyne’s Why Is God a Stranger in the Land? (14:8–9); Charles H. Spurgeon’s The Golden Key of Prayer (33:3); and Andrew Murray’s chapter “Feeding on the Word” in The Inner Chamber (15:16).
  • On Jeremiah among the prophets. Augustine’s The City of God, Book XVIII, chapter 33, on what Jeremiah foretold of Christ and the calling of the nations.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Jeremiah in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read Lamentations, the five poems of grief that follow Jeremiah in the Bible and have long been linked with his name, and Ezekiel, who was preaching the same message to the exiles in Babylon at the same time. And come back to Jeremiah in your own hard seasons. The prophet who complained most bitterly to God is also the one who heard him say, to people far from home with no end in sight:

You will seek me and you will find me, when you search for me with all your heart.

— Jeremiah 29:13
